analysis.one_liner: Bans US crude oil, gasoline, and diesel exports while the US fights Iran.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and sat in the House Foreign Affairs Committee without action after its May 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: During military operations against Iran, this bill would make it illegal for US companies to export crude oil, gasoline, and diesel fuel. The ban would stay in place until the President declares the operations over and certifies that the Strait of Hormuz is fully open to global shipping. The goal is to keep more fuel inside the United States during a wartime supply shock, with the hope that extra domestic supply pushes gas prices down for drivers. There is a narrow escape valve: the President could let crude oil leave the country if it cannot be efficiently refined here, as long as the refined fuel is brought back into the US.
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers and households paying for gasoline, diesel, and goods shipped by truck, if the ban succeeds in increasing domestic fuel supply and lowering pump prices during the war.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits US exports of crude oil, gasoline, and diesel fuel for the duration of military operations against Iran, keeping that fuel available to the domestic market.

Ends the ban only when the President declares operations against Iran have ceased and certifies to Congress that the Strait of Hormuz is fully open and global shipping through it has resumed, tying the policy to the actual supply disruption.

Includes a presidential waiver so crude oil that cannot be efficiently refined in the United States can still be exported, provided it is refined abroad and the products are imported back into the US.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers and fuel exporters, who would lose access to international buyers and the world-market prices they currently receive during the ban. If the ban reduces export revenue enough to discourage domestic drilling, consumers could eventually pay for that too.

drawbacks.text: Export bans are a blunt tool: keeping fuel home lowers the price US producers receive, which can discourage domestic drilling and shrink future supply, potentially offsetting the pump-price benefit.

The bill's own waiver acknowledges the problem: many US refineries are built to process particular types of crude, and some crude cannot be efficiently refined here, so exports would be allowed only if the fuel is refined abroad and shipped back, adding transport costs and logistics strain.
Cutting off US fuel exports during a global shock caused by the war could raise prices for allied countries and invite economic retaliation, spreading the pain rather than containing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea has a real appeal: during a war-driven supply shock, keeping fuel at home is a direct way to cushion prices at the pump, and the bill's tie-out conditions and refinery waiver show some design care. But export bans can backfire by shrinking producer incentives to drill and by forcing awkward workarounds for crude that US refineries cannot process. The bigger fact is that the idea attracted no support: not a single other member of either party signed on, and the bill got no committee action, so the trade-off was never seriously tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on May 7, 2026, referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and has sat there since with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on May 7, 2026.
It was referred to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs the same day.
No member of the House joined as a cosponsor.
The committee has taken no further action on the bill since referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and exporters, who continue selling crude and refined fuels to international buyers at world prices under the existing law the bill would have amended. Drivers awaiting the bill are no worse off than before, but they gained nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil exporters, who kept current export freedom

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban fuel exports during military operations against Iran; no colleague joined him.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill and no member of either party cosponsored it, so there was no recorded partisan split — only near-total silence from both sides.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and exporters
industries.note: The bill would cut off their access to international buyers and world-market prices whenever military operations against Iran are underway. Their interest in continuing unrestricted exports runs against the bill's goal of holding down US pump prices during the war.

Refiners would be barred from exporting gasoline and diesel during the ban, losing overseas product sales, but could see cheaper domestic crude if exports pull domestic prices down. The bill's own waiver for crude that cannot be efficiently refined in the US shows the export channel some refiners depend on would stay partly open.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee movement more than two months after introduction, the bill is highly unlikely to receive a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress. Bills without cosponsors almost never advance; it will most likely die quietly when the 119th Congress ends.
